title: SHE CALLED HERSELF A PROPHETESS. JESUS CALLED HER JEZEBEL. AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART WASN’T HER SIN—IT WAS THE CHURCH THAT ALLOWED IT.
paragraphs: SHE CALLED HERSELF A PROPHETESS. JESUS CALLED HER JEZEBEL. AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART WASN’T HER SIN—IT WAS THE CHURCH THAT ALLOWED IT.

She spoke with spiritual authority. She influenced believers. She made compromise sound like revelation. But when Jesus addressed the church in Thyatira, He exposed something far more dangerous than a woman’s deception: a congregation learning to tolerate what was destroying its soul. — Revelation 2:18–29
Imagine sitting in a church where the worship is beautiful, the people are generous, the ministry is growing, and everyone seems to love Jesus.
The prayers sound sincere.
The sermons sound spiritual.
People are serving. Families are attending. The church has a reputation for love, faith, and perseverance.
But somewhere inside that congregation, something is happening that Jesus refuses to ignore.
Someone is teaching believers that they can belong to Christ while deliberately embracing what Christ has forbidden.
And instead of confronting the deception, the church has learned to live with it.
Then a message arrives.
Not from a visiting preacher.
Not from a denominational leader.
Not from an angry former member.
From Jesus Christ Himself.
And His words are terrifying.

“Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.” — Revelation 2:20, KJV
Read that again.
Jesus did not say the church had stopped believing in Him.
He did not say everyone had abandoned worship.
He said they were tolerating something that was corrupting His servants.
And perhaps that is where this ancient letter becomes painfully personal.
Because some of the most dangerous spiritual compromises do not begin when people openly reject Jesus.
They begin when people still profess to love Him but slowly stop taking His words seriously.
And before we examine the woman called Jezebel, we need to confront an uncomfortable possibility.
What if the greatest danger to your faith is not the temptation you recognize, but the compromise you have learned to defend?
The church in Thyatira was not a congregation without good works.
In fact, Jesus began by acknowledging what was beautiful about them.
“I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.” — Revelation 2:19, KJV
Their love was real enough to be recognized.
Their service mattered.
Their perseverance had not gone unnoticed.
Their later works exceeded their earlier ones.
Yet none of those commendable qualities erased the seriousness of what Jesus was about to confront.
This is something modern Christianity desperately needs to remember.
A church can be active without being healthy in every area.
A ministry can accomplish meaningful good while still needing correction.
A believer can genuinely love Jesus and still be dangerously mistaken about what obedience requires.
Spiritual activity is not permission to ignore spiritual compromise.
And the One speaking to Thyatira was not merely another religious critic.
Revelation 2:18 introduces Him as the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like fine bronze.
The imagery is deliberate.
His eyes communicate penetrating knowledge. Nothing is hidden from His sight.
His feet convey strength and authority.
The Christ who speaks to His church is not confused by appearances.
He sees the worship.
He sees the service.
He sees the hidden teaching.
He sees what people applaud publicly and what they excuse privately.
And He sees the hearts beneath it all.
That should comfort the wounded believer who feels unseen.
But it should also sober anyone who has mistaken God's patience for His approval.
Then comes the name.
Jezebel.
A name so infamous that even people who have never studied the Bible have heard it used as an accusation.
But we must be careful here.
The original Jezebel was a queen in the Old Testament, married to King Ahab. Her story appears especially in 1 Kings 16–21 and 2 Kings 9.
She promoted Baal worship, opposed the prophets of the Lord, and was implicated in the judicial murder of Naboth.
Her influence was associated with idolatry, injustice, and hostility toward covenant faithfulness.
Centuries later, Jesus addressed a woman in Thyatira using that same name.
The Greek text of Revelation 2:20 reads, in part:
τὴν γυναῖκα Ἰεζάβελ, ἡ λέγουσα ἑαυτὴν προφῆτιν
Transliterated: tēn gynaika Iezabel, hē legousa heautēn prophētin.
The sense is: “the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess.”
The word προφῆτιν (prophētin) means “prophetess,” a female prophet.
And that detail matters.
Jesus was not condemning women simply for speaking about God or exercising spiritual gifts.
Scripture recognizes faithful women who prophesied, including Philip's four daughters in Acts 21:9. Acts 2:17–18 also speaks of sons and daughters prophesying through the outpouring of the Spirit.
The issue in Thyatira was not that the accused teacher was female.
The issue was that she claimed spiritual authority while leading Christ's servants toward conduct contrary to His will.
We should also acknowledge something important about the historical text.
Revelation does not give us enough information to establish whether “Jezebel” was her actual personal name or a symbolic designation comparing her influence to the Old Testament queen.
Many interpreters understand it as a symbolic name.
We are not told her complete biography, her appearance, her family background, or precisely how she gained influence.
And we must not invent those details.
But the accusation recorded in Revelation is unmistakable.
She was teaching and misleading Christ's servants into sexual immorality and participation in food associated with idol sacrifices.
The Greek verb translated “to seduce” in the King James Version comes from πλανάω (planaō), meaning to lead astray, mislead, or deceive.
This was not merely a disagreement about personal preference.
Jesus identified teaching that was leading believers away from covenant faithfulness.
And the setting makes the warning even more striking.
Thyatira was a city in the Roman province of Asia, known for commercial activity and trade associations.
Scholars have explored how participation in the city's social and economic life may have created pressure for Christians to attend gatherings involving pagan religious practices.
That historical context may help explain the temptation to compromise, although Revelation does not tell us exactly how the woman's teaching operated.
We should not pretend to know more than Scripture reveals.
But we can recognize the spiritual conflict.
Believers were living in a society where loyalty to Jesus could carry social consequences.
Compromise may have appeared convenient.
Accommodation may have seemed practical.
And someone claiming spiritual insight was apparently providing a way to make disobedience feel acceptable.
Does that sound completely foreign to our generation?
Think about how often people today are encouraged to redefine obedience around whatever feels easiest.
A relationship becomes more important than holiness.
Approval becomes more important than truth.
Personal desire becomes the final authority.
And the moment Scripture challenges our choices, we begin searching for someone who will tell us that God does not really mind.
Not every difficult situation has a simple answer.
Not every struggling Christian is deliberately rebellious.
Not every disagreement about biblical interpretation is deception.
But there is a real difference between a person wrestling honestly with God's Word and a teacher encouraging people to disregard it.
One is a struggle that calls for patient discipleship.
The other can become a spiritual trap.
And Jesus loved His church too much to remain silent.
What happens next is one of the most astonishing details in the entire passage.
“And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.” — Revelation 2:21, KJV
Do not rush past that sentence.
Jesus gave her time.
Time to reconsider.
Time to turn away.
Time to repent.
The One whose eyes are like fire did not immediately announce judgment without an opportunity for repentance.
He had given her space to turn.
That is grace.
Not the cheap imitation of grace that tells us sin does not matter.
Not the distorted version of grace that promises forgiveness while treating repentance as unnecessary.
But the astonishing mercy of a holy Savior who calls sinners away from destruction.
The Greek word translated “repent” is related to μετανοέω (metanoeō), which speaks of repentance—a change of mind and direction, a turning away from sin.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what happened.
It is more than crying because the consequences became painful.
It is turning toward God with an honest willingness to abandon what dishonors Him.
And here is the heartbreaking part.
She was given time.
But according to the text, she did not repent.
How many people mistake delayed consequences for divine permission?
How many assume that because their hidden choices have not yet been exposed, heaven must be indifferent?
How many interpret another ordinary morning as proof that nothing needs to change?
But the patience of Jesus is not indifference.
Romans 2:4 reminds us that God's goodness is meant to lead us to repentance.
The open door of mercy is an invitation, not an endorsement of the sin we are being called to leave.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you know needs to change, please hear the difference.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend that your struggle never happened.
He is calling you to stop making peace with what is harming your relationship with Him.
Maybe it is a relationship you keep justifying.
Maybe it is an addiction you have hidden behind a convincing smile.
Maybe it is a pattern of dishonesty that has become so familiar you barely notice it anymore.
Maybe it is a spiritual leader whose words make you feel comfortable while quietly drawing you away from Scripture.
Or perhaps you have been wounded by religious people who used accusations of impurity to control, shame, or silence you.
If so, this passage must never be used as a weapon against you.
Being tempted is not the same as teaching others to sin.
Experiencing sexual abuse is not sexual immorality on the victim's part.
And being a woman with a strong voice, leadership ability, or spiritual gifts does not make someone a “Jezebel.”
That accusation has too often been thrown carelessly at women whom others simply dislike or cannot control.
The name Jezebel is not a biblical license for misogyny, humiliation, or spiritual abuse.
Jesus' rebuke concerns specific destructive teaching and unrepentant wrongdoing.
We must honor that distinction.
Otherwise, we risk committing injustice while claiming to defend holiness.
But we cannot soften the next part of the passage either.
Revelation 2:22–23 contains severe language of judgment.
Jesus warns of a bed of suffering, great tribulation for those participating in the wrongdoing unless they repent, and judgment upon those described as her children.
The imagery is sobering.
The text does not authorize us to identify modern people as objects of this judgment or to celebrate anyone's suffering.
Nor should we confidently assign a precise medical or historical mechanism to the threatened punishment when Scripture does not provide one.
The central warning is clear enough.
Christ does not treat the corruption of His people as a trivial matter.
He declares that the churches will know He is the One who searches hearts and minds and gives to each according to their works.
In the Greek text of Revelation 2:23, Jesus says:
ἐραυνῶν νεφροὺς καὶ καρδίας
Transliterated: eraunōn nephrous kai kardias.
The expression refers to searching the inward depths of a person.
Literally, the language speaks of “kidneys and hearts,” an ancient way of referring to the deepest inner life, including thoughts, motives, and desires.
That is why translations often communicate the sense as searching minds and hearts.
Jesus is not impressed by the spiritual image we manufacture.
He knows the motives beneath our decisions.
He knows when we are confused.
He knows when we are frightened.
He knows when we have been deceived.
And He knows when we are deliberately defending what His Word has already confronted.
Yet there is another detail that changes the emotional weight of this entire passage.
Jesus does not address every believer in Thyatira as though all are equally guilty.
He speaks separately to those who have not embraced the destructive teaching.
To them, He says:
“But that which ye have already hold fast till I come.” — Revelation 2:25, KJV
Hold fast.
Two words that can feel like oxygen to a weary Christian.
Perhaps you are exhausted from trying to remain faithful in an environment where compromise is celebrated.
Perhaps you have lost friendships because you refused to abandon your convictions.
Perhaps you are trying to rebuild your life after years of spiritual confusion.
Perhaps you have fallen, repented, and are learning how to walk with Jesus again.
Hear His invitation.
Hold fast.
Not to your pride.
Not to your reputation.
Not to the illusion that you are stronger than everyone else.
Hold fast to Christ.
Because the Christian life is not a competition to prove who has never struggled.
It is a life of faith, repentance, perseverance, and dependence on the Savior who has conquered sin and death.
And this is where the story of Thyatira points us toward the heart of the Gospel.
The Jesus who confronted Jezebel is the same Jesus who spoke with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4.
He knew the truth about her complicated life.
Yet He did not treat her as disposable.
He offered living water.
The same Jesus who warned Thyatira about sexual immorality is the Jesus who forgave sinners and called them into a new life.
In John 8:11, in the traditional account of the woman caught in adultery, Jesus says, “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
That account has a well-known textual history and is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, so it should be approached with appropriate textual awareness.
Nevertheless, the combination of mercy and the call to holiness is firmly established throughout the New Testament.
Jesus does not offer forgiveness because sin is harmless.
He offers forgiveness because sinners need rescue.
He does not call us to repentance because He enjoys exposing our shame.
He calls us to repentance because He came to save us from sin.
And at the cross, we see just how seriously God takes both justice and mercy.
Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
The cross does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes transformation possible.
The resurrection does not simply promise that our story can have a better ending someday.
It announces that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That is the difference between condemnation without hope and conviction that leads to life.
Conviction says, “This cannot remain as it is.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ. Forgiveness and a new beginning are possible.”
And genuine faith does not pit those truths against each other.
It receives both.
Perhaps that is why the phrase From Scandal to Grace matters so deeply.
Because scandal is not always what other people discovered about us.
Sometimes scandal is what we finally admit about ourselves.
The jealousy we concealed.
The compromise we justified.
The secret we protected.
The bitterness we baptized as discernment.
The desire we allowed to become our master.
The truth we kept avoiding because obedience would cost us something.
And then, somehow, through the mercy of God, the heart begins to soften.
The excuses become confession.
The hiding becomes honesty.
The pride gives way to surrender.
And the person who once defended the darkness begins longing for the light.
Not because they have become their own savior.
But because Jesus Christ is changing them.
This is why we must be careful about turning Revelation 2 into a story about one wicked woman while ignoring the church that tolerated her teaching.
The text addresses both the deceiving influence and the responsibility of those who allowed it to continue.
It asks uncomfortable questions of leaders.
Are we protecting people with truth, or protecting reputations with silence?
Are we teaching Scripture faithfully, or reshaping it to avoid difficult conversations?
Are we creating communities where sinners can confess and receive loving correction, or environments where everyone feels compelled to hide?
And it asks equally uncomfortable questions of individual believers.
Who is shaping your understanding of God?
Whose approval has become more important than obedience?
When someone corrects you with Scripture, do you examine the Word honestly, or immediately search for a reason to dismiss the correction?
Are you following Jesus, or merely following voices that make Christianity easier to accommodate to your desires?
Those questions are not meant to produce panic.
They are meant to invite examination.
Because discernment is not paranoia.
Holiness is not self-righteousness.
And love is not the refusal to tell the truth.
In fact, biblical love and truth belong together.
Jesus Himself commended the love of Thyatira before confronting its tolerance of destructive teaching.
He did not ask the church to become less loving.
He called it to become faithful.
That distinction could heal many Christian communities today.
We do not need more people casually labeling others as Jezebel.
We need more believers who know Scripture well enough to recognize deception, humble themselves enough to receive correction, and love people enough to pursue restoration.
We need pastors who refuse to exploit their authority.
We need teachers who can say, “I was wrong,” when Scripture corrects them.
We need churches where sexual sin is neither celebrated nor handled through cruelty, secrecy, or favoritism.
We need communities where those harmed by abuse are protected and where allegations are handled responsibly, rather than being buried beneath appeals to forgiveness.
We need Christians who understand that forgiveness does not eliminate accountability and that repentance is not a shortcut around consequences.
Above all, we need Jesus Christ at the center.
Not celebrity personalities.
Not fear-driven accusations.
Not religious performance.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One whose Word searches us.
The One whose mercy invites us.
The One whose grace changes us.
And there is something beautiful about how the letter to Thyatira ends.
After the rebuke, the warning, and the call to hold fast, Jesus gives a promise to the one who overcomes and keeps His works to the end.
Then, in Revelation 2:28, He says:
“And I will give him the morning star.” — KJV
The promise is rich with hope.
And later, in Revelation 22:16, Jesus identifies Himself as “the bright and morning star.”

Christians have therefore long understood the imagery as deeply connected with Christ Himself and the hope of His victorious reign, though interpreters discuss the precise relationship between these passages.
Consider the movement of the message.
It begins with a church facing deception and compromise.
It confronts the reality of sin.
It announces judgment and calls for repentance.
It urges the faithful to persevere.
And it ends with a promise filled with the hope of Christ.
That is not a message of despair.
It is a message calling the church back to its Lord.
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Not another religious argument.
Not another reason to despise themselves.
Not another accusation from someone who knows nothing about their private battles.
But a moment of truth before Jesus.
A moment to say:
“Lord, I have been compromising.”
“Lord, I have been listening to voices that pull me away from You.”
“Lord, I have confused Your patience with permission.”
“Lord, I have been afraid to surrender because I do not know what obedience will cost.”
“Lord, I need Your mercy.”
If those words describe you, do not turn them into another performance.
Bring them honestly to God.
Confess your sin.
Seek His forgiveness.
Receive the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And take the next faithful step, even if it is small.
If you need to end a destructive pattern, seek wise support.
If you need to confess wrongdoing, do so responsibly.
If you have been deceived, return to Scripture.
If you have harmed someone, pursue genuine repentance and appropriate accountability.
If you have been spiritually abused, seek safety and trustworthy help. You do not have to return to an unsafe environment to prove that you forgive.
And if you have spent years believing that your past has placed you beyond the reach of God's mercy, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue in deliberate sin.
It is an invitation to come into the light through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most important question now is not whether you can identify a Jezebel somewhere in the modern church.
Perhaps it is whether you are willing to let the Word of Christ examine your own heart.
Because it is possible to spend an entire lifetime exposing the sins of others while refusing to confront our own.
And it is possible to become so consumed with identifying darkness that we forget to walk in the light.
Jesus did not give Revelation to His church so that believers could become professional accusers.
He gave His Word to reveal truth, call His people to faithfulness, and direct their hope toward His ultimate victory.
So before you leave this article, consider one question.
What have you been calling acceptable that Jesus is calling you to surrender?
You do not need to publish your private sins.
You do not need to expose intimate details to strangers.
But if this message has stirred something in your heart, I would love to hear a simple, sincere response.
Your story does not need to be dramatic to matter.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
“I was drifting. Jesus called me back.”
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message, not as a public rebuke, but as a reminder that truth and mercy still meet in Jesus Christ.
You can also invite believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown spiritually weary, and friends who are still exploring faith to follow along.
The goal is not to win an argument.
It is to help people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior continues building resources for people who want to grow deeper in their understanding of the Bible.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, understand the Gospel, and continue growing in Christ beyond a single article.
Not because a payment earns His favor.
But voluntary, prayerful generosity can still be a meaningful expression of Christian stewardship and partnership in Gospel work.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers sharing in the support of Paul's ministry, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled.
It can help support the continued creation of Scripture-centered articles, the development of discipleship resources, and the effort to reach more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
It is helping make resources available to others.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
The Gospel is.
But they can serve as everyday reminders of faith, encouragement, and the biblical truth we want to carry into our homes and communities.
A thoughtful comment may encourage another believer to keep going.
A personal invitation may help a friend rediscover the beauty of God's Word.
Because the point of Gospel Warrior has never been to make people dependent on a ministry.
It is to keep pointing people toward Jesus.
And that brings us back to the church in Thyatira.
A church that had love.
A church that had service.
A church that had faith.
A church that had perseverance.
But also a church that needed correction.
Jesus did not ignore its good works.
And He did not ignore its sin.
He loved His people enough to tell them the truth.
Perhaps that is the lesson we most need to carry away.
Christ does not ask us to choose between grace and holiness.
He calls us to receive His grace and walk in the new life that grace produces.
The scandal of our past does not have to become the identity of our future.
The deception we once believed does not have to remain the truth we follow.
The sin we once defended does not have to remain the master we obey.
Because Jesus Christ still calls people out of darkness.
He still forgives repentant sinners.
He still restores the broken.
He still strengthens the weary.
And He still says to His people:
Hold fast.
So when the world tells you that surrender is weakness, remember the cross.
When temptation tells you that compromise is freedom, remember the One who died to set you free.
When shame tells you that your story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
And when you wonder whether there is still hope for someone who has wandered so far, remember that the Savior who warned Thyatira also gave time to repent.
Do not waste the mercy of that invitation.
Come to Christ.
Hold fast to His Word.
Walk in His light.
And let His grace transform the story you thought could never change.
The most heartbreaking tragedy is not that Jesus sees the darkness we hide, but that we sometimes keep hiding from the very Savior who came to bring us into His light.
